videos.title: Europe send search and rescue personnel to Venezuela in response to massive quakes
videos.transcript: Europe is deploying rescue teams and other emergency assistance to Venezuela after double earthquakes hit the country on Wednesday leaving at least 920 people dead and more than 50,000 missing according to the UN. So far 520 responders from eight EU member states including [music] Czechia, Spain, Italy, France Luxembourg Germany Portugal and the Netherlands have mobilized for deployment through the EU civil protection mechanism. On Saturday Italian firefighters and 85 [music] French search and rescue personnel were seen arriving to join other international [music] teams in rescue operations. The UK Royal Air Force personnel prepared aid packages to be deployed to Venezuela. Meanwhile, Turkey sent two military aircraft carrying search and rescue personnel, medical teams and humanitarian aid. The two powerful earthquakes struck the northern Yaracuy region within eight minutes of each other on Wednesday night leaving unprecedented damage.
videos.summary: Following two powerful earthquakes in Venezuela's Yaracuy region on Wednesday, at least 920 people were killed and more than 50,000 reported missing. The European Union activated its civil protection mechanism, with over 500 rescue personnel from eight member states mobilizing to help. Turkey and the United Kingdom also sent search and rescue teams and humanitarian aid.

videos.title: How has Brexit changed Britain’s economy?  | The Economist
videos.transcript: How exactly has Brexit changed Britain's economy? It's been ten years since Britain decided to leave the European Union The dawn is breaking on an independent United Kingdom The country has been through six prime ministers since then and is now more divided, less influential and poorer than it otherwise might have been Brexit was a huge mistake Most economists agree that Brexit has damaged the economy Some say GDP per person is 8% lower, while others say it's only 2.5% We may not know the exact cost, but what we do know is that growth in most other big, rich countries has been faster than in Britain The effects are clearest in manufacturing Brexiteers promise to free Britain from the shackles of EU regulations They said that any trade losses with the EU would be more than made up for by greater trade with the rest of the world But that's not what's happened The value in real terms of goods traded with the EU has fallen by 7% since 2016 But trade with the rest of the world has also fallen by 6% Competition from China and high energy costs were already making life harder for British manufacturing But Brexit sped up its decline by introducing new barriers to trade with the EU, such as extra border checks and more paperwork Over 16,000 British businesses have given up exporting to the EU altogether— that's 14% of all exporters to the continent But it's not all doom and gloom Britain's exports of services have actually risen since 2016 by £62bn in the EU and £107bn in the rest of the world The biggest growth in output has been in industries with few trade barriers like IT services or advertising That has happened despite Brexit, not because of it Sectors where Brexit introduced new obstacles like financial services, they've done worse But Brexit alone can't be blamed for Britain's sluggish economy It fundamentally has the same strengths and the same weaknesses as before 2016— leaving the EU has just made everything a little bit harder
videos.summary: This video marks ten years since Britain voted to leave the European Union and examines how Brexit has affected the British economy. It looks at the impact on trade, manufacturing, and services, comparing Britain's economic performance with other wealthy countries. The video concludes that while Brexit is not solely responsible for Britain's slow growth, it has made an already difficult situation harder.

trueFalse.statement: Britain's exports of services have risen since 2016.

ordering.instruction: Put these events or ideas in the order they were mentioned in the video.

videos.title: "Good luck." Jennifer Doudna on AI Drug Discovery Promises
videos.transcript: An OpenAI executive recently suggested that if a discovery happens on ChatGPT, let's say a drug discovery, that OpenAI should get a cut of sales. What do you think of that? >> [laughter] >> Good luck. >> Expand. >> How are chatbots going to change drug discovery? I'm not sure the answer to that yet. I don't know. Lots of people are of course very, very hopeful, some very hypeful about it. Uh, but I think that innovation is still really in the domain of human beings right now. I'm not seeing chatbots in our own experience innovating. They can be helpful with summarizing data, they can be helpful in writing reports and things of that nature, but I'm not seeing chatbots uh coming up with a brand new idea for something that nobody else ever thought of. >> So, you're saying AI can't innovate? >> I don't know if it can't innovate, I just don't think it is right now. >> What about after the AGI moment? >> Well, I never say never, so maybe that'll happen, but I'm not holding my breath. >> Well, there are just so many big promises out there like Larry Ellison saying AI will cure cancer in a 48-hour window. Does that hold any water? >> Believe me, I'd be overjoyed if that is true, but I just I don't see it right now.
videos.summary: In this interview, Jennifer Doudna responds to an OpenAI executive's suggestion that OpenAI should receive a share of profits from drug discoveries made using ChatGPT. She shares her views on the current limitations of AI and chatbots in scientific innovation, and comments on bold predictions about AI curing cancer.

videos.title: Why is the UK not built for extreme heat? #Heatwave #UK #Weather #Climate #BBCNews
videos.transcript: Why is the UK just not built for extreme weather? We're just at the start of what's going to be an intense heat wave. But the reality is that the average summer temperature here is just about 16° C. With those mostly mild conditions, we're building for those conditions instead. But the future is going to be much hotter and much wetter. Large parts of our train network run on electricity and power lines sag in high temperatures. So that can mean trains get cancelled. We've also built our towns and cities with lots of rock and concrete. It absorbs the heat and then radiates it back out, making that heat even more unbearable. We're also building lots of shiny new apartments with lots of glass, which traps the heat, just like a greenhouse. And it may come as a surprise to those people not living here, but only about 5% of homes in the UK have air conditioning. All this means is that so far we haven't adapted our lives to extreme heat in the way many other countries already
videos.summary: This video explains why the UK struggles to cope with extreme heat waves. It looks at several reasons, including the country's mild average summer temperatures, the design of its cities and buildings, and the low number of homes with air conditioning. The video suggests that the UK needs to adapt to hotter and wetter conditions in the future.

videos.title: South Korea unveils $576 billion AI chip investment
videos.transcript: South Korea rolled out sweeping chip and AI mega projects on Monday. >> President Lee Jang pledged investments worth more than $576 billion over several years.
